note: The legal framework is the tree; catalogue records are the leaves (evidence-links.json). A node's status is a legal-analysis judgment, never a sum of its leaves. Not legal advice and not a finding of any court.

statuses.not_established: Not established: no sufficient supporting material yet.
statuses.partial: Partially evidenced: some relevant material, important elements unsupported.
statuses.strong: Strongly evidenced: material appears to address the requirement substantially, subject to legal review.
statuses.blocked: Procedurally blocked: a jurisdictional or procedural obstacle prevents the route unless lawfully overcome.
statuses.legal_determination: Requires legal determination: a genuine legal question an evidence score must not decide.
statuses.research_required: Research required: no verified authority yet.

nodes.label: Legal threshold
nodes.title: Legal threshold for reopening or revisiting the 1987 outcome
nodes.proposition: To disturb a final judgment there must be a recognised legal route, a court or body with jurisdiction, and grounds that meet that route's test. Fraud is not an automatic passport around finality: it has to be pleaded and proved through the route below.
nodes.status_note: A 1974 permissive-occupation mechanism is documented in the judgment. No route yet has evidence of every element needed to prove fraud, deliberate concealment or public-authority participation. The 1982–83 registration enquiry is now tied to the actual historical forms and legal framework.
nodes.applies: The decision under challenge is the Court of Appeal judgment of 31 July 1987 (EV-0080). The 1989 European outcome is a separate decision by a different body and has its own pathway.

nodes.label: Domestic courts
nodes.title: Domestic pathway: England and Wales
nodes.proposition: Routes in the English courts for revisiting BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2.
nodes.status_note: Two legally distinct routes: a fresh action to set aside the judgment, and an application to reopen the concluded appeal. They have different tests.

nodes.label: Fresh action to set aside
nodes.title: Gateway: a fresh action to set aside the 1987 judgment as obtained by fraud
nodes.proposition: An action to set aside an earlier judgment for fraud is an independent cause of action, brought by a new claim, not an application in the old proceedings.
nodes.test: The claimant must plead and prove the three Highland principles (see the Fraud branch).
nodes.standard: Balance of probabilities (see the Fraud branch on proof of dishonesty).
nodes.bars: Who may sue (Mary Williams died in 1983; William Buckler died in 1990), against whom (BP Properties Ltd or its successors), and limitation for the set-aside action itself are open questions.
nodes.uncertainty: Standing of successors, the limitation position of the set-aside claim, and the effect of later sales to third parties need specialist advice.

nodes.label: Standing and parties
nodes.title: Element: who can bring the action, and against whom
nodes.proposition: A set-aside action needs a claimant with standing in the original judgment and a defendant who obtained it.
nodes.status_note: No authority has been researched on standing of a deceased party's successors. Marked research required.

nodes.label: Limitation of the new action
nodes.title: Obstacle: limitation of the set-aside action
nodes.proposition: Where an action is based on the fraud of the defendant, time does not run until the claimant discovered it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it.
nodes.status_note: Section 32 runs from discovery, not from when the deception happened. Whether and how it applies to an action to set aside a judgment is a question for counsel.

nodes.label: Innocent purchasers
nodes.title: Obstacle: property bought by an innocent third party
nodes.proposition: Section 32 does not allow an action to recover property, or set aside a transaction affecting property, against a purchaser for value who was not party to the fraud and did not know of it.
nodes.status_note: The land has since passed to later owners. Their position is a legal question, not an evidence score.

nodes.label: Reopen the appeal (CPR 52.30)
nodes.title: Gateway: reopening the concluded appeal under CPR 52.30
nodes.proposition: The Court of Appeal will not reopen a final determination unless it is necessary to avoid real injustice, the circumstances are exceptional, and there is no alternative effective remedy. Permission is required and its refusal is final.
nodes.status_note: Probably blocked: a fresh action to set aside for fraud is itself an alternative remedy, which r.52.30(1)(c) excludes. Subject to legal advice.
nodes.test: (a) real injustice; (b) exceptional circumstances; (c) no alternative effective remedy.
nodes.bars: Permission needed (r.52.30(4)); no oral hearing as of right (r.52.30(5)); no appeal from refusal (r.52.30(7)).

nodes.label: Real injustice
nodes.title: Element: reopening is necessary to avoid real injustice
nodes.proposition: r.52.30(1)(a); the injustice must be shown to be probable, not just possible (Feakins at [12], citing Re Uddin).

nodes.label: Exceptional circumstances
nodes.title: Element: the circumstances are exceptional

nodes.label: No other effective remedy
nodes.title: Obstacle: there must be no alternative effective remedy
nodes.proposition: r.52.30(1)(c). A fresh set-aside action is the established route for a judgment obtained by fraud.

nodes.label: New evidence
nodes.title: Test: new evidence and previously unavailable facts
nodes.proposition: On an appeal, fresh evidence is admitted only if it could not have been obtained with reasonable diligence, would probably have had an important influence, and is apparently credible. In a fresh action for fraud, reasonable diligence is not required where fraud was not raised at the trial.
nodes.status_note: Which test applies depends on the route: a fresh action or reopening the appeal.

nodes.label: Not raised in 1986–87
nodes.title: Element: fraud was not raised and decided at the 1986–87 trial
nodes.proposition: Where no allegation of fraud was raised at trial, a requirement of reasonable diligence should not be imposed.
nodes.status_note: The judgment decides adverse possession and the licence letters; no allegation of fraud appears in it.

nodes.label: Credible and influential
nodes.title: Element: the new material is credible and would probably have mattered
nodes.proposition: Ladd v Marshall conditions 2 and 3; in a fraud action, materiality is tested under the Fraud branch.

nodes.label: What the 1987 decision rested on
nodes.title: Test: materiality and causation, measured against the findings the decision rested on
nodes.proposition: Materiality is assessed by the impact of the fresh evidence on the evidence supporting the original decision.
nodes.status_note: Each finding below is what new evidence has to reach. Evidence that does not touch any of them cannot be an operative cause.

nodes.label: Licence letters, no repudiation
nodes.title: Finding: the 31 October 1974 letters made her a licensee because she did not repudiate them
nodes.proposition: From receipt of the letters her possession was by licence of BP Properties Ltd, in the absence of any repudiation by her.
nodes.status_note: The judgment records that BP did not seek or wait for acceptance, but found no communicated repudiation during the relevant period. A written rejection, instructions to the solicitor, proof BP received a rejection, or a knowingly false account of her post-letter conduct would go directly to this finding. None is presently held.

nodes.label: 1962 order kept title alive
nodes.title: Finding: the 11 December 1962 order was enforceable until 11 December 1974
nodes.proposition: Time could not run against the owners while the 1962 judgment was enforceable; leave to enforce was given on 19 September 1974.
nodes.status_note: The court treated the 1962 order as enforceable until 11 December 1974 and held that the September 1974 leave application was within time. The October letters arrived 41 days before that anniversary. The timing is a documented feature; intent to manipulate the clock remains an inference.

nodes.label: BP Properties could license
nodes.title: Finding: BP Properties Ltd "had agreed to buy" and could give the licence
nodes.proposition: The court answered the "wrong company" point from the letters' own words.

nodes.label: Adverse possession 1955–74
nodes.title: Finding: the Bucklers were in adverse possession from 2 February 1955
nodes.proposition: The court accepted adverse possession from 1955 until the letters; the case turned on what happened in 1974.
nodes.status_note: This finding is in the family's favour. It also cuts against any reading that the occupation was permissive before 1974.

nodes.label: Registration not decisive
nodes.title: Finding: first registration would not have defeated a title acquired by adverse possession
nodes.proposition: The court said any title she had acquired would have bound BP's registration as an overriding interest.
nodes.status_note: The court said any title Mary had already acquired would have bound BP's registration as an overriding interest. The 1982–83 registration evidence is therefore primarily a separate rectification/indemnity enquiry, not the reason the 1987 court decided the licence issue.

nodes.label: Fraud (legal test)
nodes.title: Test: a judgment obtained by fraud (Takhar; RBS v Highland)
nodes.proposition: There must be conscious and deliberate dishonesty in evidence given, action taken, a statement made or a matter concealed; it must be material; and materiality is judged by its impact on the evidence supporting the original decision.
nodes.status_note: The 1974 unilateral-licence mechanism is documented. BP was not unaware of Mary's ownership claim: it was a party to the 1974 proceedings. The fraud question is whether BP or its solicitors knowingly misrepresented Mary's post-letter stance or withheld a communicated rejection. No such primary record is presently held.
nodes.standard: Civil standard (balance of probabilities); an inference of dishonesty needs pleaded facts that tilt the balance.
nodes.uncertainty: Whether a 1939 document can be "an operative cause" of a 1987 judgment that does not mention it is a legal question.

nodes.label: Identified act or statement
nodes.title: Element: an identified document, statement, act or concealment
nodes.proposition: The dishonesty must be in evidence given, action taken, a statement made or a matter concealed.
nodes.status_note: The judgment identifies the 31 October 1974 letters and the steps around their receipt and the withdrawn warrant. That establishes the act; it does not establish that the act itself was dishonest.

nodes.label: Falsity
nodes.title: Element: the document or statement was false
nodes.proposition: Falsity must be proved, not inferred from a gap.
nodes.status_note: Mary's 1959/1965 refusals and July 1974 ownership plea pre-date the 31 October letters; they establish a history of opposition, not by themselves a repudiation communicated during the critical post-letter period. No primary post-letter repudiation or contradictory BP account is currently held.

nodes.label: Knowledge and dishonesty
nodes.title: Element: the person knew it was false and acted dishonestly
nodes.proposition: Dishonesty is judged by the person's actual knowledge or belief, then by the standards of ordinary decent people.
nodes.status_note: The judgment shows BP knew of the 1974 ownership dispute. It does not, without the application and litigation files, establish what the relevant registration or litigation decision-makers knew or intended when making a particular statement.

nodes.label: Material to the judgment
nodes.title: Element: the dishonesty was material to the 1987 decision
nodes.proposition: The dishonest evidence, statement or concealment must be material, judged by its impact on the evidence that supported the decision.
nodes.status_note: The 1987 judgment makes the no-repudiation finding material. A proved communication to BP or a knowingly false account of it could be material; the registration process itself was not the basis of the 1987 decision.

nodes.label: Pleaded with particularity
nodes.title: Element: fraud distinctly pleaded and particularised
nodes.proposition: A dishonesty allegation must give notice of the case and be supported by pleaded facts that justify the inference.

nodes.label: Proof to the civil standard
nodes.title: Element: proof on the balance of probabilities
nodes.proposition: One civil standard applies; the seriousness of an allegation does not raise it.

nodes.label: Motive and intent
nodes.title: Evidential requirements: motive, knowledge and intention
nodes.proposition: Motive alone does not prove fraud. The evidence has to show who acted, what they did, what they knew, and that they intended to deceive, and has to rule out innocent explanations.

nodes.label: Who acted
nodes.title: Identity of the person or institution
nodes.proposition: A named person or company acting for a party.
nodes.status_note: BP Properties and BP Pension Trust are identified in the 1974 proceedings and letters. HMLR's 23 March 2026 letter identifies Linklaters & Paines as the solicitors who submitted both first-registration applications in 1982–83. Whether the firm also acted in 1974, and which individual knew what, remains to be established.

nodes.label: Evidence of knowledge
nodes.title: Evidence of knowledge of the true position
nodes.proposition: A record showing the person knew the contrary fact.
nodes.status_note: The judgment records BP's 1974 possession proceedings and Mary's ownership plea, so corporate knowledge of that dispute is evidenced. Linklaters & Paines later submitted both BP first-registration applications, but the chain from the 1974 dispute to the particular solicitor/decision-maker and what was disclosed remains unproved.

nodes.label: Evidence of intention
nodes.title: Evidence of intention to deceive
nodes.proposition: A record of a deliberate choice to mislead; inconsistency alone is not enough.
nodes.status_note: No record presently establishes an intention to deceive. The fact that HMLR later said it was unaware of an interest does not by itself prove that BP intentionally withheld it.

nodes.label: Alternative explanations
nodes.title: Alternative explanations to be excluded
nodes.proposition: Innocent readings of the same records, recorded so they can be tested.
nodes.status_note: Several held records point to ordinary explanations; they are shown as adverse leaves.

nodes.label: Deliberate concealment
nodes.title: Test: deliberate concealment (Limitation Act 1980 s.32)
nodes.proposition: Where a fact relevant to the right of action has been deliberately concealed by the defendant, time does not run until the claimant discovered it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it. Section 32 postpones limitation; it does not itself reopen a judgment.
nodes.status_note: The suspected concealment is not that BP did not know Mary claimed ownership: BP was party to the 1974 proceedings. The narrower question is whether the 1982–83 registration package failed to disclose the unilateral, disputed nature of the purported licence or represented her occupation as settled permission, leaving HMLR unaware. The applicant forms, declarations and notice records remain to be read.

nodes.label: Identified fact
nodes.title: Element: an identified fact relevant to the right of action
nodes.status_note: BP knew of Mary's claim from the 1974 proceedings. The unresolved point is whether the nature of the disputed occupation and her response to the unilateral licence were accurately disclosed to HMLR in 1982–83.

nodes.label: Held by the defendant
nodes.title: Element: the defendant (or its agent) had the fact
nodes.proposition: s.32(1)(b): concealed "by the defendant".
nodes.status_note: The 1974 proceedings establish BP's corporate knowledge of Mary's ownership claim. HMLR's 23 March 2026 letter identifies Linklaters & Paines as the solicitors who submitted both 1982–83 applications. Whether the same firm handled the 1974 letters, and what the registration team knew, must be proved from the firm files.

nodes.label: Concealed, by act or silence
nodes.title: Element: concealed by active steps or by withholding
nodes.proposition: Concealment can be by active steps or by failing to disclose; no separate duty to disclose is needed.
nodes.status_note: HMLR's 25 May 2026 letter says it did not receive or know of a family interest or possible dispute and no caution was lodged. The 30 July schedule lists the application and examination records but no item expressly described as an occupier notice. That does not prove no notice was sent; obtain any service record and read Forms 1C/1E.

nodes.label: Deliberate, not reckless
nodes.title: Element: deliberate concealment, with intent
nodes.proposition: Deliberate means consciously and intentionally; recklessness is not enough. For s.32(2) the defendant must know it is committing a breach of duty.
nodes.status_note: No primary document presently demonstrates a deliberate decision to suppress a fact with intent to conceal Mary's claim or substantiate a false claim.

nodes.label: Discovery date
nodes.title: Element: when the fact was discovered or discoverable
nodes.proposition: Time runs from discovery, or when it could with reasonable diligence have been discovered.
nodes.status_note: The 2026 letters date recent discovery of particular HMLR explanations and file schedules, not necessarily first discovery of the underlying registration or any alleged concealment. Build a separate discoverability chronology.

nodes.label: Innocent purchaser bar
nodes.title: Obstacle: purchasers for value without notice

nodes.label: Government involvement
nodes.title: Test: government or public-authority involvement and state attribution
nodes.proposition: Knowing about an event, holding records, making a decision and taking part are different things. Only participation or a decision attributable to the state, with causation, can found a claim.
nodes.status_note: The current HMLR records document later administrative responses and the Registry's retrospective account of its knowledge. They do not themselves show an official joining, directing or knowingly assisting a corporate strategy in 1974–87.

nodes.label: Knew or held records
nodes.title: Evidential level: a public body knew of events or holds records
nodes.proposition: Shows knowledge or custody only.
nodes.status_note: HMLR's 2026 letters and schedules show institutional custody and its retrospective account of the registration process. They do not establish what an officer knew in 1982–83.

nodes.label: Withheld information
nodes.title: Evidential level: a public body withheld or failed to find information
nodes.proposition: A refusal or a later find shows handling of a request; it is not proof of earlier participation. Destroying records after a request can be an offence.
nodes.status_note: The 2026 complaint responses and document schedule evidence later handling of the enquiry. No record currently shows intentional suppression, destruction after request, or an earlier official decision to conceal Mary's claim.

nodes.label: Made or influenced a decision
nodes.title: Evidential level: a public body made or influenced a decision affecting the proceedings
nodes.proposition: Needs a record of the decision and of its effect.
nodes.status_note: No contemporaneous instruction, minute, communication or decision currently links a public body to BP's 1974 licence strategy or the 1982–83 registration applications.

nodes.label: Misfeasance in public office
nodes.title: Test: misfeasance in public office
nodes.proposition: An officer exercising public power, knowing (or recklessly indifferent to) its unlawfulness and the probable loss; such conduct equates to dishonesty.
nodes.bars: Ordinary limitation applies, subject to s.32.
nodes.status_note: No identified public officer is shown to have knowingly or recklessly acted unlawfully while appreciating the probable loss to the family. Misfeasance is not evidenced.

nodes.label: Human Rights Act timing
nodes.title: Obstacle: the Human Rights Act 1998 does not reach acts before 2 October 2000
nodes.proposition: Section 7(1)(b) reaches earlier acts only in proceedings brought by or at the instigation of a public authority.
nodes.status_note: The 1974–89 events predate the Act. A Convention complaint about them lies only in Strasbourg (the European pathway).

nodes.label: European pathway
nodes.title: European pathway: application 14464/88 (Buckler v United Kingdom)
nodes.proposition: A separate pathway: the 1989 outcome was a decision of the European Commission of Human Rights, not a judgment of the Court.
nodes.status_note: No mechanism has been identified that revives a 1989 Commission inadmissibility decision. A new application would need a new final domestic decision.

nodes.label: What happened in 1988–89
nodes.title: Fact: the European Commission of Human Rights declared application 14464/88 inadmissible on 14 April 1989
nodes.proposition: Lodged 3 May 1988, registered 12 December 1988, declared inadmissible 14 April 1989 on a rapporteur's Rule 40 report, without communication to the Government.

nodes.label: Revision (Rule 80)
nodes.title: Obstacle: revision under Rule 80 applies to judgments of the Court
nodes.proposition: A party may ask the Court to revise a judgment on discovery of a decisive fact, within six months of learning of it. The 1989 outcome was a Commission decision, not a Court judgment.

nodes.label: Restoration (Rule 43 §5)
nodes.title: Obstacle: restoration to the list applies to struck-out applications
nodes.proposition: Rule 43 §5 lets the Court restore a struck-out application in exceptional circumstances; 14464/88 was declared inadmissible, not struck out.

nodes.label: A new application
nodes.title: Gateway: a new application to the Court
nodes.proposition: The Court deals with a matter only after domestic remedies are exhausted and within four months of the final domestic decision; it rejects an application substantially the same as one already examined unless it contains relevant new information.
nodes.status_note: Time ran from the 1987–88 domestic decisions long ago. A new domestic decision (for example on a set-aside action) could start a new period. Whether a Commission examination counts as "examined by the Court" under Art 35(2)(b) needs advice.

nodes.label: Exhaustion and four months
nodes.title: Obstacle: exhaust domestic remedies; apply within four months

nodes.label: Relevant new information
nodes.title: Element: relevant new information, not the same matter

nodes.label: Convention rights
nodes.title: Test: the Convention rights complained of in 1988
nodes.proposition: Articles 6, 8 and 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Commission found the fair-trial complaint unsubstantiated, the loss of the home lawful and justified, and no "possession" because the courts had held the property belonged to another.

nodes.label: Effect of a decision
nodes.title: Note: only final judgments of the Court bind States under Art 46
nodes.proposition: There is no Court judgment in 14464/88 to enforce or revise.

nodes.label: Register rectification
nodes.title: Separate remedy: rectification of the register and indemnity
nodes.proposition: Rectifying the register is a different remedy from setting aside the judgment. It can turn on fraud or lack of proper care by the proprietor, or on injustice.
nodes.status_note: The HMLR correspondence and first-registration schedule now identify the exact 1982 and 1983 file routes. The application contents and actual legal requirements at the time must be proved before alleging an inaccurate declaration or registration fraud.

nodes.label: Mistake in the register
nodes.title: Element: a mistake in the register
nodes.proposition: What was declared at first registration in 1982–83 is unread.
nodes.status_note: The separate applications, conveyances, later HMLR explanation and file schedule are documented. The actual Form 1C, Form 1E, plans and examination correspondence have not yet been read, so no register mistake is proved.

nodes.label: Proprietor's care
nodes.title: Element: fraud or lack of proper care by the proprietor
nodes.proposition: Needed to rectify against a proprietor in possession without consent.
nodes.status_note: A knowingly false statement or deliberate lack of proper care by the proprietor may matter, but the applicant's actual declaration and the title/plan comparison are not yet available.

nodes.label: Later owners in possession
nodes.title: Obstacle: today's proprietors are later purchasers in possession
nodes.proposition: Rectification against a proprietor in possession is restricted.

nodes.label: 1983 disclosure and notice rules
nodes.title: Historical law: actual occupation, cautions and disclosure in 1982–83
nodes.proposition: Apply the Land Registration Act 1925 and the Rules then in force. Section 70(1)(g) protected pre-existing rights of persons in actual occupation as overriding interests; actual occupation alone did not create ownership. The Law Commission later explained that the wording about enquiry and non-disclosure had no relevance to overriding interests on first registration. Section 53 allowed a person claiming a qualifying interest to lodge a caution which secured notice. Section 14 allowed the registrar to require the applicant and solicitor to make an affidavit or declaration about title documents, charges and material facts, but only if the registrar required it. The later Land Registration Rules 2003 rule 28 / Form DI must not be applied retrospectively. The exact 1983 Form 1C/Form 1E, any section 14 declaration and any prescribed notice must be examined before alleging a false answer or a failure to notify.
nodes.status_note: The historical framework is now distinguished from the later Form DI regime. What BP was asked, what it answered, whether the Registrar required a declaration, and what notices were prescribed by the 1983 Rules remain unknown until the original files are obtained.

nodes.label: 1925 suppression / fraudulent entry
nodes.title: Potential statutory offences: Land Registration Act 1925 sections 115–116
nodes.proposition: Section 115 addressed suppression or attempted suppression of a document or fact in registration proceedings, by a person concerned as principal or agent, with intent to conceal another person's title or claim or substantiate a false claim. Section 116 addressed fraudulent procurement of an entry on, erasure from or alteration of the register. A mistaken or unanswered application does not by itself establish either offence; the actual statement or suppression, actor, knowledge, intent and connection to the entry must be proved.
nodes.status_note: No original 1982–83 application, false answer, deliberate suppression or evidence of fraudulent procurement is presently held. These are legal tests to investigate, not findings.
